Estimation
es-tim-AY-shun
n. (a valuation set by appraisal; rendering Hebrew erek, from arak, to arrange or set in order)
From Latin aestimatio, a valuing, from aestimare, to appraise. In Leviticus it is a technical term of the sanctuary: the fixed price at which a vowed person, animal, house, or field is redeemed.

Biblical Definition

Estimation is a technical term of Leviticus 27, the chapter that governs vows. When a man devoted a person to the LORD, the person was not surrendered but redeemed at a fixed valuation: “When a man shall make a singular vow, the persons shall be for the LORD by thy estimation” (Leviticus 27:2), with a published scale following by age and sex. The scale is the ancient counterpart of a schedule of fees, and it does two things at once. It prevents the vow from becoming human sacrifice — Israel's neighbours devoted children to their gods, and this legislation makes a devoted person a redeemed person. And it prevents the vow from becoming a device of the rich, because the chapter includes a means test: “if he be poorer than thy estimation, then he shall present himself before the priest, and the priest shall value him; according to his ability that vowed shall the priest value him” (Leviticus 27:8). The poor man is not excused from his vow and not crushed by it; the priest sets a price he can pay. The firstborn are redeemed on the same principle at a fixed five shekels (Numbers 18:16), the price Mary and Joseph would have reckoned with. Behind the whole apparatus is a truth the New Testament makes explicit: persons belong to God, and what belongs to God is bought back rather than given up.

Webster 1828 Definition

A fixed valuation for redeeming what was vowed. Leviticus 27 publishes a scale so that a devoted person is redeemed rather than surrendered, and adds a means test so the poor man's vow is priced to his ability.

expand to see more

ESTIMATION, n. [L. aestimatio.] The act of estimating.

2. Calculation; computation; an adjusting of numbers or value.

3. Value; as, a thing of no estimation.

4. Esteem; regard; favorable opinion; honor.

5. In the Mosaic law, the valuation set by the priest upon persons or things devoted by vow. Lev. 27.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 27:2 — "Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When a man shall make a singular vow, the persons shall be for the LORD by thy estimation."

Leviticus 27:8 — "But if he be poorer than thy estimation, then he shall present himself before the priest, and the priest shall value him; according to his ability that vowed shall the priest value him."

Numbers 18:16 — "And those that are to be redeemed from a month old shalt thou redeem, according to thine estimation, for the money of five shekels, after the shekel of the sanctuary, which is twenty gerahs."

Leviticus 27:30 — "And all the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land, or of the fruit of the tree, is the LORD'S: it is the LORD'S holy."

Modern Corruption

The valuation scale of Leviticus 27 is read as Scripture assigning different human worth by age and sex — a misreading of a redemption tariff as a statement of value, and one that ignores what the chapter is actually preventing.

expand to see more

The objection is raised often: Leviticus 27 prices a man at fifty shekels and a woman at thirty, therefore Scripture values women at three-fifths of a man. The chapter is not appraising souls; it is setting a redemption tariff for vows, and the figures track the market value of labour in an agrarian economy, which is why they also vary by age — a man over sixty is valued below a man in his prime, and an infant lowest of all. No one supposes Scripture holds the elderly to be worth less than the young as persons; the same chapter that prices them is in the book that commands rising before the hoary head. The theological valuation is stated elsewhere and without gradation: male and female alike created in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), and both redeemed at the same price, which is not silver or gold but the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18-19).

What the chapter is actually doing is worth more attention than the objection. Israel lived among nations that devoted children to their gods in the literal sense; Leviticus makes the devotion of a person into a monetary redemption, which is why Jephthah's vow is narrated as a horror rather than a model — the law had provided him a way out he did not take. And verse 8 builds in a provision most modern legislation lacks: an obligation scaled to ability, assessed case by case by a priest who must look at the man in front of him. The rich man pays the published rate and the poor man pays what he can, and both have kept their vow. That is a more careful piece of equity than the passage's critics usually credit.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew erek (an arrangement, valuation, estimate) from arak (to set in order, arrange, lay out); the Greek Old Testament renders it time, price or honour — the same word behind the New Testament's bought with a price.

expand to see more

Hebrew erek (H6187) — an arrangement, estimate, valuation; the technical term throughout Leviticus 27.

Hebrew arak (H6186) — to arrange, set in order, lay out; used of setting the shewbread and of drawing up an army.

Hebrew ga'al (H1350) and padah (H6299) — to redeem, ransom; the two verbs governing what is done with a valued thing.

Greek time (G5092) — price, value, honour; the Septuagint's rendering, and the word in 1 Corinthians 6:20.

Hebrew cherem (H2764) — a devoted thing; the category in Leviticus 27:28-29 that, unlike a vow, could not be redeemed.

Usage

"“The persons shall be for the LORD by thy estimation” — a devoted person is redeemed, not surrendered."

"“According to his ability that vowed shall the priest value him” — an obligation scaled to means, assessed case by case."

"“For the money of five shekels” — the fixed redemption of the firstborn."
